title: Palmer Lake Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Palmer Lake wells have a 340-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $23,000-$35,800.
h1: Palmer Lake Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Well records around Palmer Lake show a predominantly Denver Basin setting, with both sedimentary and fractured-bedrock conditions affecting drilling results. The records include 3,013 permitted wells within 5 miles, although only 1,859 report total depth and 1,182 report pump yield.

For a buyer, the practical starting point is a median well depth of 340 feet and a median reported yield of 10.0 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for early planning, but a nearby well search, site-specific permit review, and a driller's bid matter more than a countywide average.

sections.heading: Palmer Lake well depth depends on the formation
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Palmer Lake is 340 feet. The middle half runs from 250 to 500 feet, so a bid near the median is not unusual, but nearby wells can differ substantially. The 90th percentile is 620 feet, and the deepest well in the records reaches 2,500 feet.

Depth records show that 51% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet. Another 25% are between 100 and 300 feet, while 13% reach 600 feet or more. The local geology includes Denver Basin sedimentary aquifers and unnamed fractured-bedrock wells. That combination is why a driller should review neighboring logs before pricing a new hole, rather than assuming every lot will match the closest address.

sections.heading: What Palmer Lake wells usually produce
sections.html:
Among wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is fairly concentrated: 83% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 14% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 3% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are reported below 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for ordinary household planning, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for the well test, pump information, permit conditions, and any production records. A buyer should also confirm the intended household use is allowed by the DWR permit.

sections.heading: Water levels around Palmer Lake and the recorded trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 120 feet below ground surface. The middle half ranges from 80 to 221 feet, which affects pump setting, electrical planning, and the amount of casing or pumping equipment a contractor may recommend.

The decade record does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 165 feet in the 1980s and 162 feet in the 1990s, then 115 feet in the 2010s and 122 feet in the 2020s. Measurements come from only 252 records, so treat the series as local historical context, not a guarantee for a specific lot. A current static-level measurement and neighboring well data are more useful when evaluating a property.

sections.heading: Palmer Lake permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity increased from the 1970s through the 1990s, with 390 permits in the 1970s, 566 in the 1980s, and 630 in the 1990s. The records show 390 permits in the 2000s, 354 in the 2010s, and 184 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

Fletcher Drilling, listed as Fletcher, Thomas, appears most often with 748 records. Kunau Drilling LLC, listed as Kunau, Timothy R., appears on 236, and Paul Fletcher & Sons Inc, also listed with Fletcher, Thomas, appears on 227. These are record counts, not endorsements. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope of work, and who will perform the test and completion work before relying on any contractor name.

sections.heading: What a new Palmer Lake well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $17,000-$23,800.

A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $23,000-$35,800. That range is for early budgeting, not a fixed proposal. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water-quality work, or changes to the pump system can alter the final price. Ask every bidder to separate drilling, casing, grout, development, testing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and permit-related work so competing bids can be compared accurately.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Palmer Lake
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported records, but a dry hole or disappointing production remains a site-specific risk. Fractured-bedrock sections can be unpredictable, and the aquifer name on a permit does not guarantee the same result on an adjacent lot. Have a driller review nearby logs and confirm the proposed well location before buying land.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 12 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These mapped sites do not prove a problem at a particular property. Test existing water for appropriate contaminants, inspect well construction and casing, and keep the well separated from septic and building areas under applicable requirements. Septic design, access, trench routes, and electrical service should be evaluated together with the well.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Palmer Lake lot
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the DWR permit, well construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and service history for the property. Compare that information with nearby records in Woodmoor and Monument, and expand the review toward Gleneagle, Larkspur, the Air Force Academy, or Perry Park when the lot is near those areas.

If the parcel has no well, budget from the local depth and finished-system ranges, then get a written site-specific proposal. Confirm the intended use, including household, stock, or irrigation needs, because permit conditions control what an exempt household-use well may provide. For a build, locate the well, septic system, driveway, house, utility trench, and turnaround together. That coordination can prevent an expensive redesign after drilling or excavation begins.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Palmer Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Palmer Lake is 340 feet. The middle half ranges from 250 to 500 feet, while the 90th percentile is 620 feet. Records include wells as deep as 2,500 feet. Because the area includes Denver Basin sedimentary and fractured-bedrock conditions, a neighboring well log is useful but cannot guarantee the depth on a particular lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Palmer Lake?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,000-$23,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $23,000-$35,800. Access, depth, casing, grout, testing, and site conditions can change the final written bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Palmer Lake?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. Records show 83% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 14% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. These are reported well results, not a guarantee for a new well or a specific pump setup.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Palmer Lake?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. The mapped area includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 12 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those locations do not establish contamination at a particular home. Test the existing water, review well and septic records, and use a qualified laboratory to select testing appropriate to the property.

faq.q: Are Palmer Lake well water levels going down?
faq.a: The recorded decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 165 feet in the 1980s, 162 feet in the 1990s, 115 feet in the 2010s, and 122 feet in the 2020s. Only 252 records report static water level, so this is background context rather than a prediction. Check the current water level and nearby wells.
